items.title: AI Is Changing Music. Its Future Must Be Built Around Artists (Guest Column)
items.summary:
At SoundCloud, we believe the future of music should be artist-first. Our brand and our business have been built on the trust artists place in us, and protecting that is fundamental to who we are. Being artist-first is the lens through which we approach AI, recognizing both its potential to expand creative possibilities and the risks it presents to artists, their rights and the communities they build. Technology will keep changing how music is made. Our responsibility to protect the artists who make it won’t.

Too often, AI is framed as a binary choice: all good or all bad, embrace it or reject it. It is time that we address this transformation with the nuance that artists deserve. The reality is that AI presents existential risks if managed wrong and game-changing opportunities if managed right. It is our responsibility to artists to both minimize those risks and maximize those opportunities.

items.title: SoundCloud CEO Talks AI Policies: ‘Wishing Away the Advent of AI Music Is Not a Strategy’
items.summary:
This year began with Bandcamp issuing a hardline stance against AI music, marking the first — and only — outright ban of AI-generated music on an online music platform. Now, it is ending with SoundCloud and its CEO, Eliah Seton , calling for a much more “nuanced” discussion of the topic.

“There’s been a very binary frame,” says Seton of the conversation around AI musicmaking and how music platforms should deal with it. “It is either good or evil, accept it or reject it.”

More than at other listening platforms, Seton appears interested in finding ways for SoundCloud to work with licensed AI music companies. In the past two weeks, SoundCloud has inked deals with Moises and ElevenLabs’ Eleven Music so that users can easily port over their AI-aided creations to SoundCloud and vice versa. These deals add to the platform’s 10 other AI music partnerships dating back to 2024 , including with Tuney, Tuttii, AIBeatz, TwoShot, Starmony and ACE Studio.

While Spotify has also eyed new opportunities with AI music, it has focused on developing its own AI-powered music remixing tool in-app, which is expected to debut early next year, rather than providing a pipeline to trusted partners.

She has had more nominations without a win than anyone else in the history of the category, a distinction she’d probably like to shed.

The list of potential replacements has been endless – but it was Pattinson who leapt to the top, his name only first connected to the role a couple of weeks ago.

Whether or not he’s been in contention all along, Pattinson does seem like the perfect Bond. For starters, he’s the right age to play a seasoned MI6 operative. items.title: Underscores live in London: hyperpop’s breakout star seizes the moment
items.summary:
Right now, putting phones away at concerts is the trendiest thing a musician can do. But Underscores doesn’t play the same game as everyone else. Tonight is the biggest headline show that the former NME Cover star has ever played in London. It’s completely sold out, and she wants everyone to witness the spectacle of her third breakout album, ‘U’ . “ So get your phones out, I like how it looks from the back ”, she sings in her intro song ‘Point A’, weaving through the backstage area until she bursts out onto the stage.

READ MORE: Underscores: “I’m trying to restore my relationship with making music” 

It’s the final show of Underscores’ European ‘Galleria’ tour – a “long ass tour”, in her words. What was supposed to be a quick 13-date jaunt ballooned when the hyperpop upstart scored a coveted support slot on Charli XCX ’s ‘Music, Fashion, Film’ arena tour in America . As such, tonight’s show feels especially hard-won: this is Underscores with arena-level training, for an esteemed gaggle of die-hard fans who’ve watched her blow up from her early SoundCloud days.

At first, it seems like it’s going to be a nonstop dance party. The scraps of her dark, witchy top fly in the air as Underscores tornadoes across the room to ‘Locals (Girls Like Us)’ and ‘Hollywood Forever’. Fans buoy the energy in the room for more minimalist cuts like the steamy ‘Innuendo (I Get U)’, while Underscores adapts the pop-punk-inspired ‘Spoiled Little Brat’ into a hardcore techno rager.

items.title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
items.summary:
Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary

Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that this physical media holds.

Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic. “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.”

items.title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
items.summary:
She threw a (metaphorical) brick through Spotify’s window and exposed industry failings with her ‘Butts for Tour Buses’ campaign. Now the singer is embracing her Irish roots with her new album’s fighting spirit

Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour.

That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’ And we didn’t.” [see footnote]

items.title: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this
items.summary:
Ulster Hall, Belfast
With two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers

‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage.

They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged into something close to peak Joe Cocker, grained at the edges, honey underneath. Lining Your Pockets is more resounding than ever.

items.title: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things
items.summary:
Bristol Beacon
The UK artist combines feminist fury with accessible melodies and a dramatic flair that sees her alternately pogoing and seeking out the wind machines at the prow of the stage

People are dancing to a song they don’t know, with flower garlands in their hair and their arms around their friends. This reaction to Fairy Dance, an unreleased track written about the community that has sprung up around her music, says a lot about the moment Paris Paloma finds herself in, and tonight’s show feels for all the world like a stepping stone to bigger things.

Throughout, Paloma leans in to the built-in drama of songs from her second album, The Fatal Flaw, which pairs ornate folk arrangements with the sort of arena-sized alt-pop production favoured by Florence + the Machine. With a sculpture inspired by surrealist Ithell Colquhoun’s Tree of Veins dominating the stage, she falls to her knees to deliver high notes and seeks out wind machines at the prow of the stage, her flowing crimson dress buffeted as if on a wintry moor.

items.title: James Blunt: ‘Do I have a nickname? Yes, it rhymes with blunt’
items.summary:
The singer on his love for Ibiza, the weirdest thing he’s done in the name of romance, and being signed up for Celebrity Traitors against his will

You were a punching bag for such a long time after You’re Beautiful became a massive hit but your consistent good humour is deeply admirable. Does it ever get tiring?

It was a surprise, at the beginning. I was just a little guy with a dream. And when you achieve your dream, you think people would be happy for you. For them not to be happy for you but angry with you, for your song, seems irrational, an overreaction. It is interesting how people generally want to tear people down for achieving their little dreams. But I’d had a real proper job before that [as a captain in the British army]. My friends might have been on operations in Afghanistan or Iraq, so if I were to complain to them at the time saying, “Oh, the Guardian said something really horrid about me and gave me three stars for my album” – they would be able to talk about who had lost their lives or limbs that day, and that put it all in perspective. And perspective is everything.

items.title: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month
items.summary:
(Erased Tapes)
Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation

Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr, in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir.

On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a haze of resonance. items.title: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul
items.summary:
After wittily blending pop and politics on their debut, the Belgians are now processing their personal lives. We join them for a mindbending tour of their home city of Ghent

Boris Kor Tom Zeebroek is staring up at a grey gothic building in the centre of Ghent, squinting through the late September sun that is covering his home town in a cloak of unseasonal warmth.

Zeebroek is encouraging his bandmate Charlotte Adigéry and I to crane our necks towards the Mammelokker, an 18th-century Flemish relief on the top of the building. It’s a gruesome bit of stone, which sits above the town square and depicts a daughter suckling her own father. The pair are taking me on a tour of their medieval home town, and this disturbing architectural decoration is part of our itinerary.

items.title: Snoh Aalegra: Legendary Love review – raw R&B talent restrained by reverence for the greats
items.summary:
(Stem)
Her truly remarkable, Sade-ish voice is hypnotic against some dizzyingly plush production, but a modern spin on 80s pastiche sometimes veers too close to tribute

Swedish-Iranian singer Snoh Aalegra has previously described her music – a lush, pastiche-y mix of R&B, hip-hop, soul and pop – as “cinematic soul”. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies, made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like the right fit.

Aalegra’s fourth album is her most successful front-to-back statement yet, even if she can’t shake off the talent-show-ish reverence for her idols. Sparse and warm, Legendary Love puts her androgynous, Sade-ish voice in dizzyingly plush environments: a hybrid of Afrobeats and 80s R&B on the hypnotic I Love You; a bed of minimalist guitars and moonlit synths on This That, which sounds as though it could have been produced by Jai Paul.
items.t: Snoh Aalegra: Legendary Love review – raw R&B talent restrained by reverence for the greats
